demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Vignette: Marama, 46

Marama grew up on the coast of Aotearoa, the youngest of five siblings, in a family where the rhythms of life were measured by the sea and by each other. She moved to Auckland in her twenties, built a career in forensic analysis, and raised two children alongside her husband, Tane. She was, by most accounts, a woman who had learned to hold difficult things steadily — her work required it. For nearly two decades she had processed evidence from crime scenes, examined data with methodical calm, and left the worst of what she saw at the laboratory door. She believed, genuinely, that she had developed a kind of professional armour.

Then, fourteen months ago, her younger brother Hemi died.

He was thirty-nine. He collapsed without warning during a Saturday morning run — a cardiac event that no one had seen coming, from a heart condition no one had known was there. Marama was the one who answered the phone. She was the one who drove to the hospital. She was the one who stood in a corridor under fluorescent lights and was told by a doctor, in careful, measured language, that Hemi was already gone by the time the ambulance arrived. She remembers the doctor's hands, the pattern on the floor tiles, the sound of a trolley being wheeled somewhere behind her. She remembers very little else from that afternoon, except that she kept thinking she needed to call Hemi to tell him what had happened.

In the weeks that followed, Marama moved through the tangihanga and the gatherings and the obligations of grief with what her family described as remarkable strength. She organised, she fed people, she held her mother while she wept. Inside, something had gone very quiet and very still, like water before a storm.

She returned to work six weeks later and discovered that the armour she had trusted no longer fit. She sits at her workstation now and finds herself unable to concentrate on chain-of-custody documentation for more than a few minutes before her mind pulls her back to that hospital corridor. When a case involves a sudden death — and in her field, they often do — she feels a pressure build behind her sternum that she cannot name. Twice she has had to leave the laboratory floor and sit in her car, breathing carefully, waiting for the feeling to pass.

She does not sleep well. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with her heart already racing, certain for a disorienting moment that something terrible is about to happen, or has just happened, or is happening now. She lies still and listens to Tane breathing beside her and waits for reality to reassemble itself. By morning she is exhausted, and the exhaustion makes everything feel slightly unreal — her children's voices, the drive to work, the ordinary texture of her own life.

She has become watchful in ways she cannot fully explain. She checks her children's locations on her phone more than she knows is reasonable. She has asked Tane, more than once, to text her when he arrives somewhere. She finds herself calculating risk in conversations, in carparks, in the bodies of the people she loves — looking for the thing that might give way without warning. Her colleagues describe her as quieter than she used to be. She does not disagree.

What disturbs her most, she says, is not the grief itself — she expects grief, understands it, has made a kind of peace with missing Hemi. What she cannot reconcile is the way his death has rearranged her understanding of the world. She had believed, without ever quite articulating it, that sudden catastrophe happened to other people's families — to the cases that crossed her desk, not to her own life. That belief is gone now, and she does not know what to put in its place. She sits with that absence the way you sit with a missing tooth — probing it, again and again, unable to leave it alone.
